title: THE PERSON YOU'RE PRAYING FOR COULD BE THE PERSON GOD IS WARNING YOU ABOUT
paragraphs: THE PERSON YOU'RE PRAYING FOR COULD BE THE PERSON GOD IS WARNING YOU ABOUT
Before You Give Someone Your Heart, Read This: The Biblical Truth About Modern Dating, Red Flags, Sexual Temptation, Emotional Wounds, and the Kind of Love That Actually Honors Jesus Christ
There is a kind of heartbreak that doesn't begin when somebody leaves.
It begins when you notice something is wrong… but convince yourself to stay.
When your peace disappears, but you call it butterflies.
When someone keeps crossing your boundaries, but you call it love.
When you cry yourself to sleep, then wake up and pray that God will somehow turn the person hurting you into the person you've always dreamed of marrying.
And perhaps the most painful part?
You knew.
Somewhere beneath the excitement, the late-night conversations, the promises, the physical attraction, and the fear of starting over…
You knew something wasn't right.
But you had already imagined the wedding.
You had already pictured the children.
You had already told your friends, your family, and maybe even your church that this person was an answer to prayer.
Now walking away feels like admitting you misunderstood God.
So you stay.
And slowly, almost without noticing, you begin sacrificing pieces of your convictions just to keep someone who has never demonstrated the willingness to protect them.
But what if the question you've been asking is wrong?
What if instead of asking, "Lord, is this the person I'm supposed to marry?" you should be asking, "Lord, who am I becoming while I'm with this person?"
Because biblical wisdom in modern dating isn't merely about finding someone who makes your heart beat faster.
It's about learning to recognize the difference between a relationship that draws you toward Jesus Christ and one that slowly teaches you to live without Him.
And that difference could change the entire direction of your life.
Perhaps you're reading this while you're deeply in love.
Perhaps you're single and exhausted from waiting.
Perhaps you're divorced, widowed, healing from betrayal, recovering from sexual sin, or wondering whether God could possibly give someone with your history another chance.
Stay with me.
Because before we finish, we're going to talk about something that many dating conversations avoid.
Not simply how to find the right person.
But how the Gospel can rescue you from losing yourself while trying to be loved.
The Bible says something remarkably direct about wisdom:
"The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding." — Proverbs 9:10 (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the opening expression is יִרְאַת יְהוָה — yir'at YHWH, commonly translated "the fear of the LORD."
This isn't merely panic or terror. In the context of biblical wisdom, it speaks of reverent recognition of God's holiness, authority, and rightful place in our lives.
Notice where wisdom begins.
Not with chemistry.
Not with compatibility tests.
Not with how attractive someone looks in their profile picture.
Not even with how strongly you feel that you've received a sign from heaven.
Wisdom begins with God.
And that changes everything about dating.
Because when God is no longer at the center of your decisions, your feelings can begin occupying a throne they were never meant to sit upon.
Feelings are real.
Attraction is real.
Longing for companionship is real.
But none of those things is infallible.
You can genuinely love someone and still be making an unwise decision about the relationship.
You can feel an extraordinary connection with someone who is not ready to build a faithful marriage.

You can even meet someone in church, hear them quote Scripture, watch them raise their hands during worship, and discover later that their private character looks very different from their public spirituality.
That doesn't mean every person who struggles is pretending.
It means religious appearance and spiritual maturity are not automatically the same thing.
Jesus warned:
"Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them." — Matthew 7:20 (KJV)
In its immediate context, Jesus is warning about false prophets. Yet the underlying principle of evaluating claims through observable fruit is relevant when discerning character.
Don't build your entire future on somebody's ability to sound spiritual.
Look at how they live.
How do they respond when they're corrected?
What happens when you say no?
Do they apologize without making you responsible for their behavior?
Are they honest when honesty costs them something?
Do they honor commitments?
Do they treat people kindly when there's nothing to gain?
Do they respect your relationship with God even when your convictions inconvenience their desires?
And perhaps one of the most revealing questions of all…
Who are they when they're disappointed with you?
Because anyone can be affectionate when everything is going their way.
Character becomes visible when love requires patience, restraint, humility, and sacrifice.
The apostle Paul describes love in words that are quoted at countless weddings:
"Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." — 1 Corinthians 13:4 (KJV)
The Greek word translated "charity" is ἀγάπη — agapē, meaning love.
In this passage, Paul describes love through qualities and actions, including patience, kindness, and the rejection of pride and selfishness.
He isn't writing a modern dating checklist. He is correcting a divided Christian community and teaching believers what love should look like.
But that makes the passage even more challenging.
Because if these qualities should characterize Christian love generally, how much more should they matter in a relationship where two people are considering sharing their lives?
Someone saying "I love you" doesn't automatically mean they're loving you well.
Love is not proven by how loudly someone claims you.
It is revealed through how faithfully they treat you.
And sometimes the person who sends you the sweetest messages is also the person who leaves you feeling constantly afraid of doing something wrong.
Sometimes the person who says they cannot live without you uses that statement to make you feel responsible for their emotional stability.
Sometimes jealousy is dressed up as devotion.
Control is called protection.
Isolation is called loyalty.
And sexual pressure is presented as proof that your relationship is serious.
But biblical love does not require you to surrender your dignity, safety, or obedience to God.
A person who loves you should not need to destroy your conscience to feel secure in your affection.
And if you're in a relationship involving intimidation, coercion, threats, violence, or repeated manipulation, please understand something important.
You are not required to remain in danger to prove that you're forgiving.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Trust requires truth, accountability, and demonstrated change.
Seeking safety and wise help is not a betrayal of Christian faith.
Sometimes wisdom means establishing boundaries.
Sometimes it means involving mature, trustworthy believers.
Sometimes it means leaving a harmful relationship and seeking professional or legal protection.
God never commanded you to make another human being your savior.
Only Jesus can occupy that place.
And this is where modern dating becomes especially complicated.
We live in a world where meeting someone can take seconds.
A swipe.
A message.
A follow request.
A reaction to a story.
A conversation that begins after midnight and suddenly feels more intimate than relationships you've maintained for years.
Technology has made connection easier.
But it has not automatically made discernment deeper.
You can know someone's favorite songs, childhood wounds, relationship history, political opinions, and dreams for the future before you've ever watched them navigate a serious disagreement.
You can become emotionally attached before you've had enough time to observe their character.
You can mistake constant communication for genuine commitment.
And when someone disappears without explanation, you can spend weeks wondering what was wrong with you.
But another person's inconsistency is not a reliable measurement of your worth.
You do not become less valuable because someone stopped replying.
You do not become unlovable because someone chose another relationship.
You do not become a failure because an engagement ended or a relationship didn't survive.
Your identity was never supposed to depend on somebody's willingness to choose you.
Scripture says:
"I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." — Psalm 139:14 (KJV)
In context, David is praising God's intimate knowledge of His creation.
This isn't a promise that every romantic interest will recognize your value.
It is a reminder that your existence is not accidental and your worth does not begin with romantic attention.
Before anyone called you beautiful, handsome, desirable, or marriage material, you were already a human being made in God's image.
Before anyone rejected you, God already knew your name.
And before you ever began searching for love, Jesus Christ demonstrated a love far greater than anything human romance can provide.
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — Romans 5:8 (KJV)
Read that again.
Christ didn't wait until you became impressive.
He didn't wait until you had a perfect relationship history.
He didn't wait until you stopped struggling with loneliness, lust, insecurity, or shame.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we finally became worthy enough to earn God's affection.
But that God's grace reached us when we could never have rescued ourselves.
And once that truth begins settling into your heart, dating changes.
You stop treating every new person as your last chance to be loved.
You stop believing that being single means being forgotten.
You stop confusing attention with affection and affection with covenant commitment.
You begin realizing that marriage can be a beautiful gift without becoming your ultimate purpose.
Because marriage is not salvation.
A wedding ring is not redemption.
And another human being cannot carry the weight of being your entire reason for living.
Jesus can save you.
A spouse cannot.
That doesn't make marriage insignificant.
It puts marriage in its proper place.
When Jesus was asked about marriage, He pointed back to God's design in creation:
"For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh." — Matthew 19:5 (KJV)
Jesus is citing Genesis 2:24, where marriage is presented as a profound union.
The Hebrew expression בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad means "one flesh."
This is much deeper than having a wedding ceremony or sharing physical attraction.
It describes a union that reaches into the shared life of husband and wife.
Modern dating, as we practice it today, isn't directly laid out as a formal institution in the Bible.
Scripture doesn't tell us which dating application to use, how many months to date before engagement, or exactly when to introduce someone to our parents.
We should be careful not to turn personal preferences, cultural traditions, or invented dating rules into divine commandments.
But Scripture gives us something more enduring than a list of dating techniques.
It gives us wisdom about holiness, love, truthfulness, sexual integrity, self-control, commitment, and the kind of character that can sustain a covenant.
And one of the most uncomfortable places that wisdom confronts us is sexual temptation.
Because our culture frequently treats physical intimacy as a casual way to discover whether two people are compatible.
But Scripture treats our bodies as morally significant.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated "fornication" is πορνεία — porneia, a broad term referring to sexual immorality.
In the surrounding verses, Paul calls believers to holiness, self-control, and honorable conduct.
Christian traditions may differ in some details of sexual ethics, but historic Christian teaching has consistently understood sexual union as belonging within marriage.
That means sexual boundaries are not simply about avoiding consequences.
They are about honoring God with our bodies and treating another person as someone made in His image.
And let's acknowledge something many people are afraid to admit in church.
This can be difficult.
Very difficult.
Especially when you genuinely love someone.
Especially when you've been lonely for years.
Especially when physical affection feels like the only moment you can finally stop feeling unwanted.
Especially when your past already includes choices you deeply regret.
But the answer to sexual temptation is not pretending desire doesn't exist.
Desire itself is not automatically sin.
The challenge is learning to bring our desires under the lordship of Christ rather than allowing them to govern our decisions.
Boundaries become much more meaningful when they are established before temptation becomes overwhelming.
That may mean avoiding situations where you've repeatedly compromised.
It may mean having honest conversations about physical affection.
It may mean choosing accountability with mature Christians who will speak truth without humiliating you.
It may mean ending a relationship where your convictions are continually mocked or pressured.
And if you've already crossed boundaries you believe God has established, please don't stop reading here.
Because shame has a terrible way of whispering that once you've fallen, you might as well remain on the ground.
It tells you that you're damaged.
That you're disqualified.
That a godly marriage is no longer possible.
That Jesus might forgive other people, but your story has become too complicated.
That is not the message of the Gospel.
The apostle John writes:
The Greek verb ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, translated "we confess," comes from a verb meaning to acknowledge or confess.
Biblical confession is not about performing shame for an audience.
It is about coming into agreement with the truth before God instead of continuing to hide.
And forgiveness is not purchased by suffering enough to make up for what you've done.
It is grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Repentance matters.
Turning away from sin matters.
Accountability matters.
But none of those things means that your past has become more powerful than the cross.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was placed in the center of a public accusation.
Her shame had become a spectacle.
Her accusers wanted judgment.
And Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those who stood ready to condemn her.
Then He said:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11 (KJV)

There is an important textual detail worth knowing. The account in John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and modern Bible editions often mark it accordingly. Christians have long treasured the passage, but it should be discussed with that manuscript history in mind.
Its portrayal of mercy and a call to leave sin behind is consistent with truths taught elsewhere in the New Testament.
And what a powerful combination those truths are.
Mercy without pretending sin is harmless.
Holiness without pretending sinners are beyond redemption.
Jesus does not offer cheap permission to continue destroying ourselves.
He offers grace that calls us into a new life.
Maybe your dating history contains mistakes you wish you could erase.
Maybe you've stayed in relationships that pulled you away from your faith.
Maybe you've used intimacy to keep someone interested.
Maybe you've lied, manipulated, cheated, or broken promises.
Maybe you were the person who hurt someone else.
Don't excuse it.
Don't minimize it.
Don't blame everybody else.
Bring it into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Make appropriate amends where possible and safe.
Receive God's forgiveness through Christ.
And begin learning a different way to love.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But there's another danger in modern dating that doesn't always look sinful at first.
It's the temptation to confuse potential with reality.
You meet someone who has a difficult past.
They seem wounded.
They speak about wanting to change.
They tell you nobody has ever understood them the way you do.
And something inside you begins believing that perhaps God brought you into their life to rescue them.
So you become their counselor.
Their emotional lifeline.
Their accountability partner.
Their constant source of reassurance.
And eventually, you become exhausted.
But you feel guilty about leaving because you think abandoning the relationship would mean abandoning God's assignment.
Please hear this carefully.
You can love someone without being called to marry them.
You can pray for someone's healing without becoming responsible for producing it.
You can encourage someone's spiritual growth without pretending that your affection can accomplish what only the Holy Spirit can do.
A relationship should never require you to assume the role of someone's redeemer.
Jesus already holds that position.
And genuine transformation is not established by tears, promises, or a dramatic apology alone.
It is demonstrated through repentance that produces lasting fruit.
Paul writes:
In context, Paul is describing the Corinthians' response to correction.
The principle matters.
Feeling sorry about consequences is not necessarily the same as turning away from wrongdoing.
Someone can cry because they're afraid of losing you while remaining unwilling to change the behavior that keeps hurting you.
So don't measure repentance only by the intensity of an apology.
Look for humility.
Look for responsibility.
Look for honesty.
Look for changed conduct over time.
And allow that change to be evaluated without rushing yourself into renewed trust.
Grace is not gullibility.
Forgiveness is not the elimination of discernment.
And Christian compassion does not mean ignoring repeated patterns of harm.
Now, perhaps your struggle is different.
Perhaps you're not dating someone who is hurting you.
Perhaps you're dating someone who is kind, respectful, generous, and genuinely caring.
But you don't share the same commitment to Jesus Christ.
And you've been wondering whether love is enough to bridge that difference.
Paul writes:
The Greek expression ἑτεροζυγοῦντες — heterozygountes conveys the idea of being mismatched in a yoke.
The immediate passage concerns incompatible partnerships between righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, and devotion to God and idols.
It does not explicitly discuss modern dating.
Still, many Christians reasonably apply its principle to marriage because marriage is one of the deepest and most enduring partnerships a person can enter.
This application should be made carefully, without turning unbelievers into villains or pretending that everyone who identifies as Christian is automatically a wise marriage partner.
A person who doesn't share your faith may possess many admirable qualities.
They deserve dignity and respect.
But shared spiritual convictions matter when you're considering a lifelong union involving worship, moral decisions, children, finances, community, and the direction of your home.
If following Jesus is central to your life, it is wise to ask whether the relationship can genuinely support that commitment.
And if you're already married to someone who doesn't share your faith, don't misuse this teaching to conclude that God wants you to abandon your spouse.
Paul addresses existing marriages between believers and unbelievers in 1 Corinthians 7:12–16 and teaches that a willing unbelieving spouse is not to be divorced simply because of unbelief.
Biblical wisdom requires reading Scripture in context.
Not using isolated verses as weapons.
And while we're talking about wisdom, let's confront another painful misconception.
Not every closed door is spiritual warfare.
Sometimes a relationship ends because two people are incompatible.
Sometimes someone isn't ready for marriage.
Sometimes serious character problems become visible.
Sometimes your hopes simply don't match reality.
And sometimes you may never receive a satisfying explanation.
It is understandable to pray for guidance through all of this.
But be cautious about claiming certainty regarding God's hidden purposes.
We cannot always say, "God removed that person because He has someone better waiting."
Scripture does not promise every believer a spouse.
It does not promise that every breakup will be followed by a more desirable relationship.
And it does not teach that marriage is the reward for becoming spiritually mature enough.
In fact, Paul speaks positively about singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
Jesus Himself lived an unmarried earthly life.
So please don't let anyone convince you that your life is incomplete because you haven't found a husband or wife.
Your calling to follow Christ is not postponed until your wedding day.
Your spiritual fruitfulness is not waiting for an engagement ring.
Your ability to serve, love, worship, disciple others, and glorify God is not dependent on your relationship status.
You can live a deeply meaningful life in Christ while single.
And if marriage eventually becomes part of your story, it should enrich a life already grounded in Him rather than become the foundation holding your entire identity together.
Still, waiting can hurt.
There are evenings when you genuinely rejoice for another couple's engagement and then go home feeling strangely empty.
There are weddings where you smile for photographs while silently wondering whether your own turn will ever come.
There are family gatherings where someone casually asks why you're still single, unaware that the question touches a wound you've been carrying for years.
And there are moments when loneliness becomes so loud that almost any attention feels like relief.
If that's where you are, I hope you'll remember this.
Your longing for marriage is not something you need to be ashamed of.
But your longing deserves to be guided by truth.
Proverbs says:
"Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." — Proverbs 4:23 (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ — netsor libbekha means "guard your heart."
In the wisdom tradition of Proverbs, the heart is not merely the location of romantic feelings. It includes the inner life from which thoughts, desires, choices, and conduct emerge.
So guarding your heart doesn't mean becoming cold, suspicious, or incapable of vulnerability.
It means taking responsibility for what shapes your inner life.
It means refusing to let desperation make decisions that wisdom would challenge.
It means being willing to ask hard questions before your emotions become deeply entangled.
Do we share a serious commitment to Christ?
Can we disagree without cruelty?
Are we truthful about our past and present?
Do we handle money responsibly?
Are we willing to seek wise counsel?
Do we respect each other's boundaries?
Can we discuss marriage, children, family expectations, conflict, and spiritual priorities without manipulation?
Are we both free to make a decision rather than being pressured by fear, guilt, or obligation?
And when either of us sins, is there genuine willingness to repent?
Those questions may not sound as romantic as watching the sunset together.
But sunsets cannot resolve dishonesty.
Chemistry cannot replace integrity.
And a beautiful wedding cannot repair patterns of contempt that nobody was willing to confront.
Dating with biblical wisdom means paying attention before making promises that will affect the rest of your life.
It means taking enough time to know the person beyond the excitement of being pursued.
It means welcoming wise counsel without surrendering your adult responsibility to make thoughtful decisions.
It means praying without treating every emotion as a prophetic revelation.
It means allowing truth to interrupt fantasy.
And it means recognizing that the purpose of Christian dating isn't to see how close you can get to sin without crossing a technical line.
It is to consider whether a relationship can move toward marriage in a way that honors God and respects both people.
That requires maturity.
And maturity sometimes sounds like this:
"I care about you, but we need to slow down."
"I forgive you, but trust needs to be rebuilt."
"I am attracted to you, but I won't violate my convictions to prove it."
"I want to understand you, but I cannot accept being insulted or threatened."
"I would rather face the pain of an honest ending than build a marriage on dishonesty."
And sometimes…
"I love you, but I cannot continue this relationship."
Those are not easy words.
They may come with tears.
They may disappoint people.
They may require you to surrender a future you've already rehearsed in your imagination.
But biblical wisdom is not measured by how painless your decisions are.
It is measured by whether those decisions reflect reverence for God, faithfulness to His Word, and love grounded in truth.
And here's something else we need to remember.
The wisdom you want in another person should also be growing in you.
It's easy to create a list of qualities we expect from a future spouse.
Faithful.
Patient.
Emotionally mature.
Prayerful.
Honest.
Forgiving.
Responsible.
But are we learning those qualities ourselves?
Do we apologize when we're wrong?
Do we honor other people's boundaries?
Do we tell the truth even when it makes us uncomfortable?
Do we handle rejection with dignity?
Do we seek God's help with our own jealousy, lust, pride, anger, and insecurity?
Do we treat someone kindly even after realizing we don't want to pursue a relationship?
Are we becoming the kind of person who knows how to love without controlling?
Because biblical dating wisdom isn't only about identifying red flags in others.
It's also about allowing God to confront the things in us that need to change.
Jesus says:
"But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." — Matthew 6:33 (KJV)
In context, Jesus is addressing anxiety over material necessities such as food and clothing.
This verse should not be twisted into a promise that if you seek God first, He must give you the spouse you desire.
Its central command is far more profound.
Seek God's kingdom first.
Let His righteousness shape your priorities.
Trust Him with the needs and uncertainties of your life.
Even your romantic future.
Especially the parts you cannot control.
And if the relationship you hoped would last forever has already ended, I want to speak to you for a moment.
You may have lost more than a person.
You may have lost the future you imagined.
The names you planned for your children.
The house you pictured.
The anniversary dates you thought you would celebrate.
The feeling that somebody had finally chosen you.
And now ordinary things hurt.
A song.
A restaurant.
A familiar street.
A photograph you can't bring yourself to delete.
You might even feel embarrassed because you prayed so confidently about that relationship.
But grief does not mean you lacked faith.
And needing time to heal does not mean you're failing God.
Bring that grief to Jesus.
Not the polished version.
Not the version that sounds impressive during prayer meetings.
The real one.
The version that says, "Lord, I'm angry."
"Lord, I don't understand."
"Lord, I still miss them."
"Lord, I'm afraid I'll never love again."
The Psalms are full of honest lament.
God's people have never been required to pretend their hearts aren't hurting.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (KJV)
That verse does not guarantee instant emotional recovery.
But it reminds us that brokenhearted people are not beyond God's concern.
And sometimes the beginning of healing is simply admitting how much it hurts.
Not rushing into another relationship.
Not checking whether your former partner has moved on.
Not using another person's attention to anesthetize your grief.
Just bringing your wounded heart into the presence of the Savior.
And letting wise people walk beside you.
Because you don't have to process every heartbreak alone.
There is a reason Christian community matters.
There is a reason counsel matters.
There is a reason accountability matters.
Not because other believers can make your decisions for you.
But because love can sometimes make us less willing to notice what is plainly visible to those who care about us.
Proverbs 15:22 says:
"Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established." (KJV)
Seek counsel from people whose lives demonstrate wisdom, honesty, humility, and faithfulness to Scripture.
Not merely people who will agree with whatever you've already decided.
And not people who pressure you into staying in unsafe situations.
Wise counsel helps you see more clearly.
It does not take away your dignity or agency.
Now imagine something with me.
Imagine a relationship where you don't have to hide your love for Jesus.
Where prayer isn't a performance.
Where disagreements don't become opportunities for humiliation.
Where affection doesn't require sexual compromise.
Where apologies are followed by genuine efforts to change.
Where both people understand that love isn't always a feeling of excitement.
Sometimes love looks like patience after a difficult day.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth when lying would be easier.
Sometimes it looks like admitting, "I was wrong."
Sometimes it looks like refusing to retaliate.
Sometimes it looks like choosing faithfulness when nobody else is watching.
And sometimes it looks like two imperfect people kneeling before a perfect Savior, admitting that neither one is capable of loving well without His grace.
That is not a promise of a conflict-free marriage.
No relationship between sinners will be perfect.
But it is a picture of love being shaped by the Gospel rather than merely by desire.
And this brings us to the heart of everything.
The greatest love story in Scripture is not about two people finally finding each other.
It is about Jesus Christ coming to redeem sinners who could never save themselves.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He loved with a purity we have failed to demonstrate.
He spoke truth without sin.
He gave Himself on the cross for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Paul summarizes the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4:
"Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures." (KJV)
This is the center of Christianity.
Not relationship advice.
Not personal success.
Not finding a perfect spouse.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And through Him, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by grace.
That includes the person who has been sexually immoral.
The person who has cheated.
The person who has been dishonest.
The person who has made romance an idol.
The person who has compromised convictions out of loneliness.
The person who has used someone else's affection selfishly.
The person who has spent years hiding behind a religious appearance.
And the person who feels too ashamed to believe that God could still welcome them.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Jesus is a sufficient Savior.
The cross exposes the seriousness of sin.
And the resurrection announces the victory of Christ.
You do not need to pretend your past never happened.
You need to bring your past, your present, and your future under the lordship of Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
And learn to walk in newness of life.
Perhaps today, the most important dating decision you can make has nothing to do with sending a message, accepting a proposal, or ending a relationship.
Perhaps it is finally surrendering your heart to Christ.
Not so He will owe you a marriage.
Not so He will guarantee a particular person will return.
But because He is Lord.
Because He is worthy.
Because His love is greater than the approval you've been chasing.
And because following Him is worth more than keeping a relationship that requires you to turn away from Him.
If this article has exposed something you've been hiding, you don't have to confess private details publicly. But I want to invite you to respond honestly.
Your story, shared with wisdom and respect for others' privacy, may encourage someone who believes their life is beyond redemption.
Not because every sentence will be easy to accept.
But because there may come a night when loneliness begins negotiating with convictions you once held firmly.
And you may need to read these truths again.
You may never know whose heart needs encouragement today.
This ministry exists to point people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, conviction, encouragement, repentance, healing, and discipleship.
These resources are intended to help you study the Word, strengthen your faith, understand the Gospel, and continue growing long after you've finished reading this article.
And I want to extend a personal invitation to those who believe this work is worth sustaining.
It is a practical way to help sustain and expand this work so more people can encounter biblical teaching, discipleship resources, and the message of salvation through Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
That matters.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be driven by guilt, spiritual threats, or the belief that God's acceptance can be purchased.
You can glorify God through generosity in many ways.
It's the opportunity to participate in sharing biblical truth.
Because somewhere, someone is reading Christian content while sitting in a relationship that is breaking their heart.
Someone is struggling to believe Jesus could forgive their sexual past.
Someone is terrified of being single.
Someone has stopped praying because shame convinced them that God no longer wants to hear their voice.
And someone may be only one faithful explanation of the Gospel away from understanding that Christ offers real forgiveness and new life.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not withholding His grace from anyone who cannot afford a monthly contribution.
We give because we have received grace, not to purchase it.
And that distinction must never be lost.
Before you go, I want you to remember the question we began with.
What does biblical wisdom look like in modern dating?
It looks like refusing to let attraction silence discernment.
It looks like loving people without worshiping them.
It looks like honoring sexual boundaries without despising those who have fallen.
It looks like recognizing that forgiveness does not require accepting ongoing harm.
It looks like choosing character over charisma.
Truth over fantasy.
Holiness over temporary approval.
And the lordship of Jesus Christ over every romantic dream.
It looks like remembering that a beautiful relationship is not necessarily one without hardship, but one where both people are committed to truth, faithfulness, repentance, and growing in love.
And if your story has already gone terribly wrong…
If you have loved unwisely…
If you've compromised…
If you've been betrayed…
If you've betrayed someone else…
If you're sitting in the wreckage of a future you thought God had promised…
Please remember this.
Your story is not beyond the reach of Christ.
You may need to repent.
You may need to forgive.
You may need to seek help.
You may need to grieve.
You may need to walk away.
You may need to spend a season learning how to live faithfully without a romantic relationship.
But you do not need to surrender to hopelessness.
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance also offers forgiveness and new life to those who come to Him in faith.
And whether your future includes marriage or singleness, your greatest hope is not that another person will finally choose you.
Your greatest hope is that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose again, and is able to save those who come to God through Him.
So pray for wisdom.
Walk in truth.
Guard your heart.
Love with integrity.
And above all, follow Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not losing someone you wanted to spend your life with. It is losing sight of the Savior who gave His life to redeem yours.
